domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is primarily about LLM evaluation methodology, judges, test suites, and measuring quality—directly matching evaluation_testing_benchmarking. The evaluation methodology discussed applies across all AI application verticals without focusing on any single domain. The talk covers testing via test suites and evaluators, plus monitoring through production log mining and alignment tracking over time. Requires basic familiarity with LLM applications and software testing but introduces evaluation-specific concepts for practitioners. A presented conference talk at the AI Engineering Summit. Multiple transcript evidence anchors with grade 'said_in_transcript' directly support the classification.

summary: The speaker, co-founder of HoneyHive (an evaluation tooling company for AI engineers), presents at the AI Engineering Summit. Previously he led the data and ML platform team at Templified, a Series D enterprise startup. After working with hundreds of teams—from two-person startups to Fortune 100 enterprises—across use cases like multi-agent systems, text-to-SQL, and RAG, he observed recurring evaluation problems that standard testing frameworks cannot handle. He defines evaluation as having three core components: (1) the agent being evaluated, (2) the dataset of inputs and ideal outputs covering happy paths and edge cases, ideally written by domain experts, and (3) evaluators measuring quality. LLM-as-judge has become popular due to dramatic improvements in speed, cost, and consistency (over 80% agreement with human judgments). However, two major problems exist. Criteria drift occurs when evaluator criteria from popular frameworks like RAGAS, Promptfoo, and LangChain don't align with specific use case requirements. Dataset drift occurs when carefully crafted test suites fail to represent messy, context-dependent real-world inputs. The speaker then prescribes a three-step iterative alignment approach. First, align evaluators with domain experts by having them continuously grade outputs and critique evaluator results, using their feedback as few-shot examples in evaluator prompts. He strongly recommends binary scales over Likert scales and stresses customizing evaluator prompts rather than relying on templated metrics. Second, keep datasets aligned with real-world queries by logging production interactions and automatically flowing underperforming queries back into the test suite—Hamish and others have written extensively about this. Third, measure and track alignment over time using F1 scores for binary judgments or correlation coefficients for Likert scales, via a simple dashboard. He recommends involving domain experts early (even 20 examples in spreadsheets), building an eval console for experts to iterate on evaluator prompts, and treating evaluator prompts as evolving artifacts. The goal is continuous improvement, not perfection. LLM evaluations are only as good as their alignment with real-world usage; teams must not treat tests as static like in traditional software.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Speaker introduces himself as co-founder of HoneyHive, previously led data/ML platform at Templified. After working with hundreds of teams from startups to Fortune 100s across diverse use cases, he observed recurring evaluation problems that standard testing frameworks cannot handle.

sections.title: Fundamentals of Evaluation
sections.summary: Defines evaluation as having three components: agent (what you evaluate), dataset (inputs and ideal outputs covering edge cases, written by domain experts), and evaluators (how you measure quality). Notes these are dynamic and must evolve over time.

sections.title: Rise of LLM Evaluators
sections.summary: Explains why LLM-as-judge is popular: speed (8–10 hours down to under an hour), cost ($3–$20 vs. several hundred per thousand ratings), and consistency (over 80% agreement with human judgments). References NLG-Eval and SPADE papers.

sections.title: Problem: Criteria Drift
sections.summary: Criteria drift occurs when evaluator's notion of good no longer aligns with user's. Popular frameworks use generalized criteria. Shares e-commerce example where standard relevance checks missed real user needs. References Berkeley's EvalGen paper by Shankar's team on balancing true/false positives.

sections.title: Problem: Dataset Drift
sections.summary: Dataset drift occurs when test suites lack real-world coverage. Users ask messy, context-dependent questions combining multiple queries in unanticipated ways. Metrics may look good but don't represent reality—like practicing for a marathon on a treadmill.

sections.title: The Fix: Three-Step Iterative Alignment
sections.summary: Prescribes three steps: (1) Align evaluators with domain experts by having them continuously grade and critique outputs, using critiques as few-shot examples in evaluator prompts; (2) Keep datasets aligned with real-world queries by logging production interactions and flowing underperforming queries back into test suites; (3) Measure and track alignment over time using F1 scores for binary judgments or correlation coefficients for Likert scales. Emphasizes this is less work than dealing with meaningless evals.

sections.title: Practical Recommendations and Conclusion
sections.summary: Recommends customizing LLM evaluator prompts rather than relying on templated metrics, strongly preferring binary scales over Likert. Involve domain experts early—even 20 examples in spreadsheets helps. Read production logs to find real-world failures and add them to test banks. Treat evaluator prompts as evolving artifacts, not sacred texts. Build an eval console for domain experts to iterate on evaluator prompts. Set up dashboards to track alignment scores. The goal is continuous improvement, not perfection. LLM evals are only as good as alignment with real-world usage; don't treat them as static tests. Speaker closes by inviting connections on LinkedIn and pointing to HoneyHive at honeyhive.ai.
